name: twin
intent: Give one logical entity two independently evolving parent hierarchies by splitting it into a pair of closely linked objects, each extending one parent, each answering that parent's protocol and forwarding the messages that belong to the partner, so both protocols are satisfied without multiple inheritance.
problem: One thing must be a first-class member of two hierarchies the language will not combine: its abstraction's hierarchy (game items, widgets, domain entities) and the platform or framework hierarchy that owns its runtime behaviour (thread or task, window base class, persistence or lifecycle base class). The language lets a class extend only one of them, yet clients of each hierarchy receive the entity through that hierarchy's own protocol, and both aspects have to be created, updated and retired together.
context: Languages whose classes have exactly one superclass but whose parents carry code and state (Java, C#, Modula-3, Oberon-2), or any design where two independently owned hierarchies cross in one entity - a framework base class plus the application's own type hierarchy. Applies when the second protocol is imposed by a framework you cannot change and when both parents' code, not only their signatures, must be reused.
benefits: Both protocols are genuinely supported: each end is a real subtype of its parent, so existing containers, registries and dispatch points accept it (the ball belongs to the list of game items and to the list of threads).
Parent code is reused on both sides while each hierarchy keeps evolving on its own: neither parent needs to know about the other.
Name clashes and diamond ambiguity disappear, because the two parents' members live in two different objects instead of one merged class.
The structure extends to a third parent as a third end, so an entity can be assembled from hierarchies owned by different teams or frameworks.
Replacement is local: either end can be substituted (or stubbed in tests) through the parent protocol it implements without touching the other hierarchy.
Full framework compatibility: no parent base class has to be refactored, wrapped or made virtual for the pair to work.
tradeoffs: Two objects per logical entity: identity, equality, hashing and locking must be defined explicitly, and every client has to know which end it holds and how to reach the other.

The pair must reach into each other's internals (package-private fields or module-internal access), so encapsulation is deliberately widened for the pair and both ends have to live in one package or module.

The mutual references form a cycle: where the runtime does not collect cycles one link must be weak or cleared, and differing lifetimes (short-lived abstraction end, long-lived platform end) otherwise leak or dangle.
Construction and teardown must be atomic - the pair is valid only when both links exist, so creation belongs in one factory and destruction needs a defined order.
Forwarding is hand-written: every message that crosses from one hierarchy to the other becomes a delegating method that must be kept in step, and a call across the link cannot be inlined.

Re-entrancy is easy: a platform callback that calls back into the abstraction end while it is mid-update interleaves state unless an explicit guard (the paper's suspended flag) or lock ordering is used.
Observability splits: debuggers, logs, heap dumps and serializers show two objects where the design means one, and tooling will not connect them.

participants.responsibility: Existing class or interface whose code and protocol the entity's primary end must reuse - GameItem in the originating example, a widget or domain base class in practice.
The second parent, usually owned by a framework, carrying the runtime behaviour and state the entity must inherit - Thread, a window/view base class, a persistence or lifecycle base class.
Subclass of Parent1 that answers and overrides Parent1's protocol, adds the entity's own members, and holds the reference to Twin2 for the messages that belong to the other protocol.
Subclass of Parent2, mirrored: it answers Parent2's protocol (run, paint, lifecycle hooks) and forwards the messages that belong to Parent1 to Twin1.
Factory or static creation method that builds both ends, links them in both directions and returns the end the caller asked for, so no half-linked twin can ever be published.
Code that holds one end through the parent protocol it already uses (the item list, the scheduler's thread list) and reaches the partner only through the twin link when it needs the other end.

use_cases: Simulation and game objects that must be scene items and runnable tasks at the same time - the originating example: BallItem extends GameItem while BallThread extends Thread.
UI toolkit components that must extend the toolkit's widget base class and still participate in an independently designed model, command or lifecycle hierarchy.
Domain objects that must extend a framework base class carrying code and state (mapper, workflow engine, actor runtime) while remaining members of the application's own type hierarchy.
Middleware and plugin objects that have to be registered in the container's component base class (lifecycle callbacks with code) and in the application's type hierarchy at once.
Automation and device control: an entity that is both an element of a UI tree and an element of a scheduler or worker list, with clicks and ticks kept in step.
Test seams: keeping one end replaceable by a test double while the other end stays a real framework object.

The Java Design Patterns catalogue ships a runnable open-source implementation of the pattern in package com.iluwatar.twin: BallItem extends GameItem and BallThread extends Thread are wired with mutual setTwin setters, a volatile isSuspended flag guards the crossing calls, and click() on the item end suspends or resumes the twin's run loop - the canonical modern reference implementation.

Java AWT's heavyweight Component/ComponentPeer pairing is the closest mainstream twin-like construct: each Component holds a transient peer field and each native peer holds its target component back, so the Java-side object and the native-window-side object live in two disjoint hierarchies, forward messages across the link, and are created and disposed together - described by practitioners as twin-like, though the toolkit-managed link is one-directional composition.
avoid_when: The second parent is a pure interface or protocol with no state and no behaviour: implement it directly instead of splitting the object.

The language provides the capability itself - multiple inheritance (C++, Python), traits with state (Scala), modules as mixins (Ruby), class-expression mixins (JavaScript, TypeScript), embedding plus interfaces (Go), protocol extensions (Swift) or interface delegation (Kotlin). Use that instead of simulating it.
Only one hierarchy is polymorphic and the other is just a collaborator: plain composition with one-way delegation is simpler and has no cycle.
The crossing protocol reduces to events: register the partner as an observer or listener instead of creating a second object of the entity.
The two aspects never need each other's protocol: keep two independent objects and no twin link.
The thing has no identity of its own: for value-like data (amounts with units, ranges, coordinates) a value object or record avoids the split entirely.
anti_patterns: Twin as a general composition flavour: splitting ordinary classes into two linked objects so the framework's extension points need not be learned - pairs that forward everything and own nothing.
Half twins: constructing one end alone or re-linking at runtime, so some clients find a null or stale twin reference.
Strong cycles that never break: reciprocal strong references between a long-lived platform end and short-lived abstraction ends, so neither side is ever collected.
God twin: accumulating every field on one end while the other becomes a hollow shell, so the pair no longer represents two hierarchies.
Subclassing only one end: deriving new subtypes on Twin1 without keeping Twin2's protocol in step, which breaks the pair's invariants and its dispatch contract.
Using twin to sneak past a framework's intended extension point by working around final or sealed base classes instead of using the supported hook.
design_principles: Composition over inheritance for the crossing link: the two hierarchies are joined by references and forwarding, not by a shared superclass.
Single responsibility per end: each end owns exactly one parent protocol, which is what makes the split work at all.
Separation of concerns: abstraction behaviour and platform behaviour evolve on their own; the twin link is the only seam that has to stay in step.
High cohesion and low coupling: the pair is a closed collaboration inside one package or module, and no other code needs to know both ends.
Least knowledge: a client should talk to the end belonging to the hierarchy it already uses, not to the partner.
Interface segregation in disguise: the two protocols stay separate types, so clients of one hierarchy never see the other's members.
best_practices: Create both ends in one place - a factory, a static creation method or a pair constructor - and make an unlinked twin impossible (private constructors plus a link step, or a factory that owns the wiring).
Return the end the caller asked for and expose the twin link as narrowly as the language allows (package-private field, internal property, private accessor); never hand both ends to ordinary clients.
Decide explicitly where state lives: state inherited from a shared base is duplicated per end by construction, so single-copy state belongs in one end and is reached through the link.
Keep the forwarding surface minimal, one method per crossing message and grouped per protocol; forward intent, not the partner's whole API.
Prefer a weak or clearable reference in the direction of the shorter lifetime, and define a teardown order that survives either end being dropped first.
Guard re-entrant crossing calls with an explicit state flag (suspended/active) or a lock ordering rule, and document which end may call which during a transition.
Test the pair as a unit with a fixture that asserts both links, and keep a separate test that the entity still behaves correctly through each parent protocol.
Keep both ends in one package or module and record the widened access in the design notes, so the encapsulation concession stays visible.
sources: Mössenböck, H. (1999). Twin - A Design Pattern for Modeling Multiple Inheritance. In: Bjorner, Broy & Zamulin (eds), Perspectives of System Informatics (PSI 1999), LNCS 1755, Springer, pp. 358-369 - the originating description, written in GoF catalogue form (Java/Modula-3/Oberon-2 motivation, the BallItem/BallThread example, participants and consequences).

Talwar, P., Harandi, M. (1993). A Systematic Approach to Multiple Inheritance Implementation - https://doi.org/10.1145/152739.152749, the 'twin objects' predecessor: an instance inheriting A and B represented as a linked pair of subobjects, each twin holding a reference to the other.
